spans.text: Every lesson of the road with Hamo, Xezo and Hevalo, in words and pictures.
I am Hamo, and every line of this road is mine: in the app you hear me say it, and here you can read it at your own pace, with a pencil, in the shade of a tree if you have one.

The road runs through Sêvan, a village of apple orchards under the mountains. You will not find it on a map: Sêvan is a made-up village, drawn from the villages of the Kurdish countryside, with their flat roofs, their springs and their walnut trees.

Read everything aloud, even when you are alone. Kurdish lives in the mouth, not only on the page. And when a word will not stay in your head, go back to the app, listen, and say it after me. What you still remember on the second day is yours.

One more thing. If you meet a young deer with round cheeks near the apple trees, that is Hevalo, your guide. He will tell you he is not hungry. Watch the apple in the corner of the page as you go through a chapter, and judge for yourself.
Every lesson opens with its little scene. Read it first: it tells you where you are and who is up to what.
The line in the speech bubble is Hamo’s. Say it out loud, as he says it in the app, until it comes out by itself.
New words come with a picture where there is one. A small m or f marks a masculine or a feminine noun: Kurdish cares.
Kurdish stands on the left and English on the right, everywhere. Cover the right side with your hand and see how far you get.
Each chapter ends with a story, pencil practice, and a stamp for your passport. The answers wait at the back.

Hamo was born in Kobanî and grew up with Kurdish roots, and later built his life in the Netherlands. Like many Kurds who grow up far from their homeland, he came to see how much a language holds: who a people are, their culture, and what passes from one generation to the next. So he created the Hevalo app, to make learning, practising and keeping Kurdish easier and more of a pleasure. On the road he is your host in Sêvan.

Hevalo brings you to Hamo’s blue gate in the first lesson and walks the whole road beside you. His name means “O friend!” Curious about everything and quick on his feet, he hops when he is pleased, tilts his head when something puzzles him and pricks up his ears at anything new. When apples go missing, he is always the first suspect.

Xezo is the young teacher at the village school. She comes from Amed and teaches the children of Sêvan their letters, and she lives in the village like any other neighbour. Bright, quick and kind, she knows the city and the village alike.

Hevalo, a young deer with a twitching nose and a weakness for apples, brings you up a lane of apple trees to a blue gate in Sêvan, a village of orchards under the mountains. Behind it lives Hamo: born in Kobanî, owner of the proudest black moustache in the valley and of more tea glasses than chairs. The neighbours come to tea at Hamo’s: Nazê from next door with her son Baran, nine and full of questions, and her daughter Hêvî, six and shy until she isn’t, and then Dapîr Şemsê, the village grandmother, who leans on her stick and on everybody. On the guest-room wall hang photos of Hamo’s family, far away in Kobanî. Hêvî counts the hens with Dapîr and gets a different number every time; breakfast is spread on a cloth on the floor and Hamo puts five sugars in his tea; everyone says which animals they have, and Bozo the donkey puts his big grey head over the wall to make sure nobody forgets him. Hevalo has no apples, and makes sure everybody notices.

Hamo shows you his house, all the way up to the flat roof where everyone sleeps on summer nights, and the clay tenûr in the yard where Dapîr bakes bread. You learn the colours of the village (the blue gate, the red apples, the green leaves, Dapîr’s white goat) and where things are: on, under, in, in front of and behind, while Hevalo hides apples in every one of those places. A game of “touch your nose” goes wrong when Hevalo joins in, and an apple shared under the walnut tree by the spring loses its other half to a certain deer. Then Hamo walks you through the village: the school, where Xezo, the young teacher from Amed, teaches the children their letters, the shop, the spring and the hills. Tomorrow is market day in the town.

After all that govend Hamo’s back has given up, and he turns out to be the most dramatic patient in the valley. The neighbours fuss, Nazê brings soup, and the doctor who comes up from the town, Doctor Azad, an old man with a kind voice and no patience for nonsense, examines Hamo from top to toe. ”), and, once Hamo is back on his feet, a moustache contest at the tea house, with comparisons and superlatives flying. Honey is forbidden; a jar goes missing; a moustache is sticky. At breakfast Baran finally tells what happened yesterday: he took Bozo to the river, Bozo saw a goat across the valley and ran off, Baran ran after him, got lost among the rocks, sat down under a walnut tree and fell asleep, and came home in the dark by the stars, to find that Bozo had been home for hours, eating Dapîr’s mint. Then everyone tells their own yesterday, and the days of long ago: Hamo as a handsome young man with a black moustache, the wolves that roam around the village when it gets dark and the bears and foxes of the forest, and Dapîr’s summers on the pastures as a girl. A message comes down from Bişar the shepherd: something wild and shy, like a deer, comes to his tent every night. Hevalo’s ears go straight up, and Hamo decides that this summer everyone goes up to the zozan. Then Bozo runs away again, and is found at the spring with Ferhad’s little donkey, very much in love.

The shepherd on the path is Bişar, Hamo’s old friend, and he leads everyone up to the zozan, the high summer pastures, where his black tents stand by a cold spring. Life up there is milk and bread and work: milking at dawn, churning butter in a goatskin, baking bread on the saj, songs at night under more stars than Baran can count. Following the two deer, the camp finds a hidden lake and an old stone house: Dapîr’s summer home when she was a girl, where, she remembers, a young flute player from Kobanî used to play for the shepherds by the lake. My name is Mohamad Saleh Abdulrahman. I was born in Kobanê and grew up with Kurdish roots, and later built my life in the Netherlands.
Like many Kurds growing up outside their homeland, I came to understand how important language is to preserving identity, culture and the connection between generations.
This inspired me to create Hevalo, a platform built to make learning, practising and preserving the Kurdish language more accessible, engaging and enjoyable.
I believe Kurdish is more than a language. It carries our history, our stories and expressions, and the experiences of the generations before us.
This book is one small contribution to keeping that heritage alive, and to making it easier for future generations to discover, learn and embrace their language.
